175: [edit] A lulav whose leaves are separated from each other but did not become loose like palm leaves is kosher even if it is not bound. Rem"a: However, it is the preferrable way to do the mitzvah to have a lulav whose leaves are totally separated (the Maggid, the Ra"n ch. "Lulav haGazul").

[edit] Iכ its leaves burst — that is, they became loose from the spine of the lulav like palm leaves, (meaning that they do not rise from the spine and instead hang down (the Maggid ch. 8) — it is invalid. Rem"a: And obviously [it is invalid] if its leaves burst and were uprooted from under the spine, in which case it is invalid even if bound (Tur, Ra"n ch. "Lulav haGazul"). Similarly, if the leaves became hardened, like wood, and it is impossible to attach them to the spine, it is invalid (Tur and Beit Yosef). All of this refers to a majority of the leaves. But if a minority became that way and the rest of the leaves remain and the lulav is still covered in leaves, it is kosher (Ra"n ch. "Lulav haGazul").

[edit] A lulav leaves grows like this: when they grow, they grow in pairs attached together from the back. The back of these sets is called the tyomet. If the tyomet is split (in most of the leaves) (Tur, Beit Yosef) it is invalid. If the leaves grew individually from the beginning, such that there is no tyomet, or if all double leaves are on one side and the other side has no leaves, it is invalid. Rem"a: Some interpret this as meaning that if the central top leave on top of the spine is split across the spine, it is considered a split tyomet and is invalid, and this is our practice (Trumat Hadeshen 97). However, ab initio it is the preferred way to do the mitzvah to get a lulav whose top leave is not split at all, because there are those who are stringent when even some of it is split. If that leave is not double from the beginning of its growth, it is invalid (Kol Bo).

[edit] If the leaves were not one on top of the other like lulavs are but rather one below the other, if the head of one reaches the stem of the one above it such that the whole spine of the lulav is covered in leaves, it is kosher. If the head of one does not reach the side of the stem of another or there are not many leaves on top of each other, just one from each side reaching the stem of another, it is invalid.

[edit] A lulav where the majority of leaves have dried out (or its spine) (Tur) is invalid. The measure of dryness is when the greenness is finished and it whitens. Rem"a: Some say that it is not considered dried until a fingernail can disintegrate it due to its dryness (Tur quoting Tosafot) and this is the practice in these countries, where there are not palm trees (Hagahot Maimoni ch. 7).

[edit] If the top [of the lulav] was severed, meaning that most of the top leaves are severed, it is invalid. Rem"a: If the top central leave on the spine was severed, it is invalid (the Maggid, Ra"n ch. "Lulav haGazul"), assuming there is another [lulav]. If there is no other one, we bless on this one (Mordechai ch. 3 and Minhagim).

[edit] If it cracked and the two sides are so separated that it looks like two, it is invalid. Rem"a: Even if the top tyomet is not split such that the lulav would be invalidated because of the split tyomet.

[edit] If it has thorny things on its spine, was smashed, shrunk, or bent forwards such that its spine was like the back of a hunchback, it is invalid. Similarly, if one side was bent, it is invalid. But if it is bent backward, it is valid, because this is how it grows.
[edit] If it is bent at the top, it is invalid. This is specifically when its spine is bent. However, if its leaves are bent at the top, as they are in many lulavs, it is valid.
